lines: At seven forty two on an ordinary Tuesday morning, every woman and every girl on Earth disappears.
About four billion people. No warning. No explanation.
This is not a prediction. It is a thought experiment. And its purpose is simple. To see how much of the world quietly rests on them.
Hour one. Silence. And then the phones.
Millions of calls, to numbers that will never ring again. In kitchens, cups still warm. In cars, seat belts still buckled. In hospitals, beds with no one beside them.
Day one. The hospitals.

According to the World Health Organization, women are about seventy percent of the world's health and social care workforce. Twenty four million of the world's twenty eight and a half million nurses and midwives.
Wards run on a handful of staff. Operations stop mid way. Every patient, of every kind, is suddenly less safe.
Week one. The schools.
Worldwide, about ninety four percent of pre primary teachers, and around two thirds of primary teachers, are women. Classrooms close.

And at home, a harder fact. The International Labour Organization counts sixteen point four billion hours of unpaid care work every single day. Women do seventy six percent of it. Cooking. Cleaning. Caring for children, the sick, and the old.
That work appears in no budget. And it stops, all at once.
Month one. The food, and the economy.

Women are about forty three percent of the agricultural workforce in developing countries, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization, and often feed their families first. Harvests are missed.
And roughly two in five of the world's workers are gone. Factories, banks, shops and offices run half staffed. Supply chains, built for a full workforce, begin to break.
Be clear about one thing. Men are capable of learning every one of these jobs. Many would, with extraordinary effort.
The problem is not ability. It is scale, and speed. Four billion people cannot be replaced in a week. Or a year.
Year one. The hardest losses have no statistic.
Four billion people are not a workforce. They are mothers, daughters, sisters, wives, friends, doctors, teachers and neighbours.
Every surviving man has lost someone. Many have lost everyone. The world does not just run short. It mourns.
Year ten. Here the thought experiment becomes arithmetic.

No women means no new births. Frozen embryos exist, but they need a womb to grow. And no technology can carry a human pregnancy from start to finish outside a body. Artificial wombs have kept lambs alive for weeks, and have never been used for a full human gestation.
The last children born are already growing up.
Year fifty. A world of older and older people.
No children are born. Schools stand empty for lack of students. Care homes, with no one left to care. Global life expectancy is around seventy three years.
Every year, there are fewer of us.
Year one hundred, or a little more. The last person alive turns off a light.
A species that spent three hundred thousand years building everything we know, ends in about a century. Because half of it was gone.
That is the thought experiment. And its point is not despair. It is respect.

The World Health Organization found that women are about seventy percent of health workers, and hold only around a quarter of senior roles. The ILO values unpaid care work at roughly nine percent of global output, about eleven trillion dollars, and most of it is done by women.
A world that depends on them this much should see them this much.
Nobody disappears. Not today. But every day, in small ways, we can see the work. Thank the person doing it. Share it. Pay for it. And stop calling it nothing.
Think of the woman whose absence would change your world. Tell her, today. Then say her name in the comments.
Notice the work.
